segments.text: A man lies in the snow, high on Everest, under a crust of ice. His team has left him for dead. Twice. Fifteen hours later, he opens his eyes.
Dead twice? No chance. Let's go look.
Case fourteen. May the tenth, {1996|nineteen ninety six}. Beck Weathers is a pathologist from Dallas, and he is climbing Everest with an expedition led by Rob Hall.
High on the mountain, something goes wrong, and it isn't his legs. It's his eyes. He has had eye surgery, and up here, at this height, his sight is going. He can't see well enough to climb on.
So he stops. Some accounts say his leader told him to stay put. Others say he chose to. Either way, he waits for the leader to come back for him. He waits for most of the day.
The leader does not come back. Rob Hall dies on the mountain, in the storm that is already on its way.
At last Weathers starts down with a group of climbers. And then the blizzard hits them.
In the dark and the wind they cannot find the high camp. They are close to the tents. They just can't find them. I've lost my hat in less wind than this.
In the night, rescuers reach them. They judge that Weathers is beyond help. That is the first time he is left.

Next morning a doctor from his own team goes out to him. He finds him under the ice, still breathing. But there is nothing he can do for him up there, and he has to leave him too. That is the second time.
He was not alone out there. Another climber, Yasuko Namba, lay beside him. She did not survive.
The news goes down the mountain. A report written at Base Camp that week says a doctor had confirmed his death. His wife is told that he is dead.
And he just lies there. By his own count he is unconscious for about fifteen hours. Other accounts say sixteen, or eighteen. I wouldn't have bet on any of them.
That afternoon, he wakes up. His right hand is bare, and frozen solid. By his own account, what gets him up is a vision of his family.
So he stands up. And he walks, on his own two feet, into the camp his group could not find the night before.
Even now, nobody thinks it changes much. They put him in a tent, make him comfortable, and expect him to die in the night.
Morning comes. He is still alive. That's three times this mountain has been wrong about him. I'm starting to feel better about my own record.
Now he has to get off the mountain. His hands are frozen, by one report to the elbows. With help, he goes down on foot to a lower camp.

What comes next is one of the highest helicopter rescues flown up to that time. An army pilot, Lieutenant Colonel Madan K C, sets down above the icefall. One report from that week puts it at about twenty thousand feet.
Two climbers are flown off the mountain. Beck Weathers is one of them.
It costs him. His right hand, and part of the forearm. The fingers of his left hand. Parts of both feet. And his nose, which surgeons rebuild.
He goes home to his family. And he writes a book about it. He calls it Left for Dead.
Not everyone came home. Rob Hall, Yasuko Namba, and other climbers died in that storm. This case file is theirs too.
Left for dead twice. Written off a third time. He got up anyway. I was wrong. Case closed.
